I have farmed these lands in Quzhou for over forty years. I am sixty now, and because I finished high school — which was uncommon in my village when I was young — I have always read the agricultural bulletins and followed the extension station's advice. I own ten mu of good flat land with well water, and I know this soil better than I know my own hands.

This year I will stick to the wheat-maize double cropping system. It is the backbone of the North China Plain, and at my age I do not have the energy or the risk appetite to experiment with vegetables or specialty crops. The winter wheat was sown last October with improved varieties, and it is greening up now. My focus in spring is to topdress nitrogen at jointing, irrigate three more times after the winter irrigation I already applied, and keep watch for powdery mildew and aphids. I expect about 520 kg per mu if the weather cooperates. After harvest in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid summer maize using no-tillage direct seeding — there is no time to waste between crops, and the stubble helps keep moisture in the ground. For the maize, I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing, side-dress urea at the big trumpet stage, irrigate twice, and control weeds and the corn borer. I target 580 kg per mu. Some younger farmers talk about growing garlic or chili for higher prices, but wheat and maize have stable government minimum purchase prices, subsidies, and I already own the combine and the seeder. This system feeds my family and pays for my grandchildren's schooling. That is enough for me.
